parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys was up early and angry with his boy for lying abed and forgetting his lute, then spent the morning at his office. After dinner he met Lord Brunker and Commissioner Pett at Gresham College about Mr. Castle's ship draft, and he took great pleasure in their discussion and in Pett's ability. Late that evening, a letter from Plymouth brought news that two of the fleet's ships were lost aground in the Straits and others nearly were, with a Dutch fleet heading there. He called this most sad news, and on returning home he was much troubled to learn that his canary bird of three or four years had died.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys attended a Committee of Tangier at Whitehall, where Lord Ashley proposed that Povy continue as Treasurer until his accounts were settled. Later at Whitehall he gave the Lord Treasurer and others an account of the Navy's shortage of money, and they could offer only helplessness, leaving him vexed. At Lady Batten's he joined merry company and played with Lady Pen, then went home to supper with his wife, merry though still vexed.

parsed.narrative.summary: In the morning Pepys attends a Committee of Tangier, where Lord Ashly's vexation with Povy's accounts leads to a proposal that Povy continue as Treasurer. In the afternoon at Whitehall he gives the Treasurer and others a large account of the Navy's charge and want of money, and receives no real answer. He goes home vexed, then spends the evening merrily with women at Lady Batten's and at supper with his wife, though he is vexed.

The next morning he hears news of a fleet engagement and a captain's legs being shot off, then hears the contrary, that all were well and the Royal Katherine is sound.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys was anxious before his Tangier Privy Seale was reviewed by Lord Privy Seal, but it passed at first reading and he was received civilly. Back in London, after dinner and a visit to Gresham College, Povy gave him discouraging news about getting money and suggested Backewell might have designs on the matter. Pepys fell into a cruel melancholy at the thought of losing what he had almost in hand, and his hopes from Mr. Warren also looked doubtful. He went home to his office and supper with his head aching, and went to bed around 10 or 11.

This left Pepys in a cruel melancholy about losing what he had nearly secured. He then consulted Creed, met Mr. Warren with doubts about his protection, and went to bed with a headache.
canon.narrative.meaning: Money will be hard to get, and his prospects may fail.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rises, speaks sternly to his boy's lute-master about the boy's neglect of lute and singing, and spends the morning and afternoon busy at the office. On Sunday 23 April, the Coronation day, he takes his wife to Whitehall Chapel and hears the young Stillingfleet preach a plain, honest sermon that he admires. After dinner at Povy's he finds Povy's excessive praise of his house off-putting, and an afternoon walk and an evening of music with friends follow. A dispute with Captain Taylor over a corant ends with the two parting friends, and Pepys and Creed laugh about it after Taylor leaves.

In Drury Lane he saw plague houses marked with red crosses, a sad sight that left him in an ill conception of himself and his smell, and he bought roll-tobacco to smell and chew, which relieved the apprehension.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the day at the office and dines with Coll. Cleggat, feeling merry and content. He is troubled by sick and discharged men left outside the office with no ships or money to take them. After dinner he gives the poor some words and money, and later goes home to his wife, who is out of temper. She tells him of a quarrel with her maids, and he grows angry and jealous, starts to leave, then turns back to bed. He resolves to smooth the matter over rather than pursue it, and ends the month with great content, though the plague remains a worry.

He then dines with Sheriff Hooker, arranges an insurance matter with Sir W. Warren, and notes with worry that his parish has the greatest number of deaths in the city. He goes home with his mind at rest.

salience.tether.stake: the city's safety and money owed to him

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walks to Lambeth on a fine frosty morning and spends an hour on Navy business before dining with Lord Bruncker and Sir Ellis Layton, all merry. In the afternoon he sees his seamstress at the Exchange and pays for thread stockings. That night, after a supper with Mrs. Penington, he walks in the cold dark while she undresses for a planned portrait, then returns home and is pleased with his recent money matters. He ends the day troubled by the rising sickness and, most of all, by an account so tangled over two months of Tangier dealings that he has not reconciled it for three or four months.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He fears he will hardly ever come to understand his accounts thoroughly again, as he used to when he was at home.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the morning at the office and dines merrily with colleagues, including Mr. Evelyn, in good humour. Back at the office in the evening he writes letters and goes home with his head full of business and some trouble over letting his accounts go so far. He swears an oath that night to drink no wine until he has passed his accounts and cleared all.
